Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01106

I suspect that Avicenna argued this way to make room for the view held by Aristotle’s followers, rather than because it was the account he himself would have given. Otherwise, he would have had to answer several objections to ideas he and other philosophers defend. The first is that we can choose the first option: the potential intellect itself becomes actual when the abstract form is present, just as the sense power becomes actual when a sensible form is present. Avicenna asks whether the form is understood because it is present in the intellect in any way, or because it is present in something capable of understanding.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01107

The right answer is the latter: it is understood because it is present in a being that can understand. We are not trying to define or explain the cause of how an abstract form is understood, so this does not make a thing explain itself. The point is that an intelligible form exists in the potential intellect differently from the way a natural form exists in matter. Matter cannot understand, and forms mixed with bodily features cannot be understood as they are. But abstract forms can be understood by the potential intellect because it can receive them. Another way to put it is that the potential intellect understands an abstract form because it is present as something without position to a being that also has no position.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01108

Second, the potential intellect is the human rational soul. If it becomes the intelligible form in act, it seems that the human being changes into a separate intellect. Avicenna rejects this kind of change between substances, especially when neither substance is material. But the soul’s existence can grow stronger, as we have explained in our discussions of potentiality and change.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01109

Third, the number of separate intellects would increase every time a potential intellect became actual. There would also be many individuals of one human kind without matter or any connection to matter. Fourth, Avicenna’s claim that an intelligible form does not need another intellect to understand it depends on saying that the potential intellect knows itself as something able to understand. But, in their account, the potential intellect is not a separate being whose own reality is present to itself in this way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01110

Anyone who accepts this high and subtle teaching must examine many basic questions about reality and depart from the path followed by most people. That is what happens when someone seeks the truth about God and leaves behind the familiar resting places. God knows best.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01111
XXVIII. First Principles, Their Relation to Later Principles, and the Defense of the First Principle
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01112

First principles cannot be learned through definitions or proofs. In our understanding of things, there are basic ideas such as existence, thing, and being present. These cannot be defined, because they have no parts and nothing is clearer than they are. In our judgments, a first principle is that affirmation and denial cannot both be true of the same thing, and that one or the other must be true. This principle cannot be proved. Any proof of it would go in a circle.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01113

A proof establishes one claim by showing that, if it is true, something else must be true, and if it is false, something else must be false. But if a proof could itself be neither true nor false, it would not prove anything. So a proof of the first principle would already depend on the principle being true. If we tried to prove it through another claim, we would end up proving it by itself. The other basic and reasoned judgments all depend on this first principle. It is the starting point of judgment and needs no further proof.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01114

The Necessary Being is pure, unrestricted existence. A possible thing, by contrast, has a limited kind of existence. To say “this is a sphere” means that it exists as a sphere and not as a human, plant, animal, or some other kind of thing. A possible being has a limited existence because it is not all other kinds of existence. In the same way, every judgment other than the first principle is that principle with some added condition. To say “everything is either necessary or possible” means that everything is either necessary or not necessary, or possible or not possible. This is the first principle stated with a particular subject.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01115

For example, “the whole is greater than its part” means that the whole’s being greater than its part is not false, so it must be true; both truth and falsehood cannot be absent. The claim that things equal to one thing are equal to each other also depends on the first principle. If things of the same kind are equal to one thing but not to each other, their nature would have to be the same and different at once. The claim that one thing cannot be in two places at the same time follows in a similar way: if one thing were in two places, it would not differ from two things there. The second thing would then be both present and absent. So these two judgments depend on the claims that truth and falsehood cannot both hold, and that one or the other must hold. The same analysis applies to other basic and reasoned judgments.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01116

This is why philosophers and other thinkers agree that a person who denies this first principle cannot be persuaded through debate. They give three possible explanations. The person may not understand the terms. Or the person may stubbornly refuse to accept the principle. Or arguments leading to opposite conclusions may seem equally strong, leaving the person unable to decide which is right.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01117

In the first case, explain the meanings of the terms. In the second, some philosophers propose beating or burning the person, saying, “Being beaten and not being beaten are one; being burned and not being burned are one.” I say that a case of this kind belongs to a physician, not a philosopher. Such obstinacy is not simply a lack of developed understanding, as one might find in children, some women, or people whose capacities are limited. It may come from an illness that the physicians of the time attributed to excess black bile, disturbing the brain. They would treat it as they treated melancholy.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01118

In the third case, the remedy is to resolve the person's doubts. Begin with geometry and arithmetic, move to the rules of logic, then to the principles of natural science, and only gradually to what lies beyond nature. Pure theology should come last. Most people should not attempt these difficult studies at the outset. Very few are equipped to understand them, and success comes from God, the Mighty and Wise.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01119
XXIX. Every Separate Being Must Understand Itself
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01120

Once we understand knowledge as existence present to a thing without absence or concealment, it is easy to show that every separate being understands itself. Matter does not perceive itself, because it has no existence apart from form. Natural forms do not perceive themselves either: their existence is bound up with bodies and places, and each part is elsewhere than the others. A body cannot be present to itself as a whole. But a being that is not bodily is present to itself, and therefore understands itself. Knowledge is existence without being hidden from the knower.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01121

What hides a thing is, in truth, absence. To be free of concealment is to exist so fully that one's being is not weakened by the lack and limitation found in lesser things. We have also proved that every form actually understood by the soul understands itself, even if there is no other intellect in the world to understand it. Every immaterial form, whether it has been freed from matter or has never been material, is itself intelligible in this way. It therefore understands itself. This establishes what we set out to prove.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01122
The philosophers have offered four arguments for this conclusion.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01123

The first is Avicenna’s argument. He first argues that when an intellectual form becomes one with the potential intellect, it makes it intellect in act. If such a form can make another thing an actual intellect by being present to it, then a form that exists by itself is all the more an actual intellect. Heat makes something hot, so heat by itself would have the power to heat; whiteness makes something visible, so whiteness by itself would be even more visible. As we have seen, the argument he gives for the first claim is weak. If that part fails, this next step fails too.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01124

The second argument is close to the one we gave at the start. Whatever is free of matter and its effects is present to itself. Whatever separate form is present to a separate being is understood by it. So every separate being understands itself. A thing either exists through itself or depends on another thing. Avicenna says it is meaningless to suggest that it simply exists without being present to itself. We have already explained how a presence between the thing and itself is possible even though the two are not separate.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01125

We know ourselves directly, and we do not have two selves, one that knows and one that is known. We are one self. This shows that knowledge does not always require two separate sides. A separate being is a fully abstract form, and a fully abstract form is intelligible in itself. When it is present to itself, it understands itself.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01126

The third argument comes from the author of The Illuminations. He says he learned it from the spiritual presence of Aristotle in a subtle state like a dream. He told Aristotle that the question of knowledge was difficult. Aristotle replied, “Look within yourself and the difficulty will be resolved.” The author said, “How?” Aristotle asked whether he knew himself through himself or through something else. If it were through something else, there would have to be another self or power that knows, and the question would return. So, he knew himself through himself. The author asked if this happened because his self left an effect in itself. Aristotle said: if the effect did not match your self, then it would not be your image, and you would not know yourself. The author agreed that the effect must be an image of himself. Aristotle asked if that image was the self without any added features or the self with other features. The author chose the second. Aristotle replied that every image in the mind is universal, even if it combines many universal ideas, because it can still apply to more than one thing. But your self is unique and cannot be shared. So you do not know yourself through an image.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01127

The author then suggested that he knew the concept “I.” Aristotle replied that the meaning of “I,” as a concept, can apply to many people. “I,” “we,” and “he” have universal meanings when separated from any particular person. The author asked how, then, he knew himself. Aristotle answered: you know yourself neither through another power nor through an image, whether or not it matches you. Your self is the intellect, the knower, and what is known. The author later summed this up: knowing is the presence of a thing’s form to a being free of matter; more fully, it is the thing not being hidden from that being. Since the soul is free of matter, it is not hidden from itself. It knows itself to the degree that it is free of matter. When it cannot bring a real thing such as the sky or earth into its presence, it brings an image of it into the soul. Particular images are held in the soul’s powers, while universal ideas are present to the soul itself. The image present in the mind is what we directly know, not the thing outside the mind. We call that outside thing universal only in a secondary sense. This account seems to agree with Avicenna that the soul’s powers do not themselves know particular things, though we have already explained why we disagree.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01128

The fourth argument is that every separate being can be understood. This is clear: every thing can become intelligible either by its own nature or after the mind abstracts it from matter. Someone may object that human beings cannot fully understand God. The obstacle, however, is not God, whose reality is supremely clear, but the limits of our own understanding. We know only as much as our powers allow.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01129

This also answers an objection from The Investigations. If God’s reality were existence itself, someone might say, and existence is something we can understand, then we could understand God fully. But existence as a general idea is not the real existence of anything, still less God. The philosophers do not mean that God and possible beings share one reality and differ only through added features, so that possible beings would have more reality than God. Every kind of existence and every perfection comes from God. Existence is good, and the greatest good is God Himself. Absence and limitation are forms of evil. When we say that God is not a body, we do not mean that He lacks something good; we mean that He is free of the limits and harms that come with a body.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01130

If a separate being can be understood, it can also understand. When one separate form is present to another, their forms are together in the intellect. This possibility must belong to what they are, not depend on the intellect’s prior act of receiving them. Otherwise, the possibility of their being together would depend on their already being together, which makes no sense. So a form that exists on its own can be present to every other form, and can understand them. And since understanding anything includes awareness of the self that understands, every separate being can understand itself and other things.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01131

In the realm of beings free from matter, whatever is genuinely possible is already actual. There is no matter there, and no motion through which something can pass from an undeveloped ability to a completed one. Such beings have no perfection still waiting to be gained. This is how the argument establishes that the Necessary Being knows both Himself and other things. For the Necessary Being, existence is necessary in every respect: whatever can truly belong to Him must belong to Him by necessity.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01132

Philosophers who use the second argument first show that God understands Himself, then show that He knows other things because He is their cause. Those who use the fourth argument first show that He knows other things, then say that His knowledge of them means He knows Himself. These two arguments move in opposite directions. I think the second part of the fourth argument is difficult to defend by the usual rules of logic. First, the fact that an individual can exist does not show that every possible thing of the same kind can exist, unless the kind applies in the same way to all its individuals. A mental image may differ from the outside thing in some features, such as being present in the mind, as these philosophers say. Perhaps the relation between intellectual forms is like that. Also, features that belong to a thing only as it is in the mind—such as being universal or shared—do not apply to the outside thing. We can also say that “being together” is a broad, unclear kind of relation. It does not follow that every specific kind of being together is possible. A physical image, for example, cannot be together with a separate intellectual form in the same way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01133

Second, the rule fails because nothing can be together with God in this way. How, then, can this argument prove that God knows things? It can do so only if one accepts that images of things exist in God’s being. Third, the argument would require every separate intellect to contain actual forms of every possible thing. That would give even the First Effect more distinct aspects than can be counted. It would also conflict with the philosophers’ view that each separate intellect has no more than two or three aspects. In short, this argument is hard to apply and does not succeed as it stands. Even if it did, it would work only if we accepted that intellect means the union of the knower and the known, and that God contains all things in the highest and most complete way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01134
XXX. Every Separate Being Is Intellect in Itself
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01135

This does not need a new proof. Every argument we have given for the first claim shows that a thing’s understanding itself cannot be separated from its being understood by itself. The fourth argument can also show this. If a separate being can understand something else, it must also understand itself. Since it is free of matter and its effects, anything it can know must already be present to it in act. It cannot be changed by an outside influence or move from potentiality to actuality. Nothing new can arise in it. So if it can be understood, it must already be understood. And because it can understand every thing that is open to its understanding, it must understand itself. Every separate being is therefore intellect in itself, always.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01136

A contemporary of Avicenna raised an objection. The human soul understands universal ideas, so it must be a separate substance. If every separate being is intellect in act, the human soul must already be intellect in act, but it is not. If you say that the body keeps the soul from acting, the body must also help it understand, which seems to be true. Avicenna replied that not everything free of matter is intellect in act. It must be completely separate: matter must not make it what it is, bring it into being, or give it the features that prepare it to become actual intellect. The proof applies only to a being separate from matter in this complete sense. It is not strange for one thing to block one action while helping with another.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01137

I do not think this answer settles the matter. Avicenna and his followers say the human soul is already a separate substance in its own being, though the body helps bring about its particular existence. The body is not part of the soul’s essence. If the earlier proof works for every separate being, it should show that the soul can understand every intelligible without any obstacle from its own nature, even if we imagine the body and all its distractions removed. But that cannot be right. Children and people with little education would not suddenly know every truth if we took away their bodies and all their distractions.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01138

The better answer is that the human soul is not intellect in act at the start of its life. It is free of natural matter and bodily forms, but it still depends on images. Most arguments that prove the soul is separate show only that it is separate from the natural world. A soul is fully separate at the intellectual level only when it can understand universal ideas as universals, and can grasp the true unity and simplicity of intellectual reality. Only a few people reach this level.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01139

Apart from our life of sense, the soul has two further levels: imagination and intellect. When the soul’s ability to imagine becomes complete, it becomes an actual imaginer. It is then separate from the world of sense and from the bodies, places, and directions found there. Its images are not physical things that can be pointed to. When its ability to understand grows through sound proofs and clear definitions, it becomes intellect in act and is separate from both the sensible and imaginal worlds. It can then understand any reality or essence it chooses. What was only potential when the soul was at the imaginal level has now become actual intellectual form.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01140
XXXI. How the Active Intellect Relates to Our Souls
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01141

We have seen that the human soul rises from one form and level of perfection to another. It begins with simple bodily existence, then takes on the forms of the elements, minerals, plants, and animals, until it develops all the powers of animal life. It then reaches the first level that is not tied to bodily matter. As it rises further, it reaches the acquired intellect, the first level fully separate from matter. This is close to the Active Intellect. The acquired intellect contains forms that were first joined to matter and later became separate. The Active Intellect, by contrast, was never in matter and must always be separate.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01142

It is surprising that the acquired intellect and the Active Intellect are of the same kind, since one depends on the other. The Active Intellect takes the self that is intellect only in potentiality and makes it intellect in act. It also makes forms that were understood only in potentiality—forms held in imagination—understood in act. A thing cannot make itself move from potential to actual. What does not exist cannot become actual unless something already actual brings it into existence. A body cannot heat itself; it needs something hot. It cannot light itself; it needs something that gives light. So the Active Intellect relates to the potential intellect as the sun relates to the eye in darkness. Sight is a power that is ready to see but needs light. The eye alone is not enough to make sight actual, and colors alone are not enough to be seen. The sun gives light to the eye and to the colors. The eye then sees, and the colors become visible.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01143

In the same way, the Active Intellect, which is always actual, gives the potential intellect a kind of existence. That existence is to the intellect what light is to sight. Through it, the potential intellect understands that existence itself and understands the Active Intellect, which gives it this intellectual light. Through it, forms that were understood only in potentiality become understood in act, and the soul becomes intellect in act. Those forms also become actual intellects.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01144

Our account also says that a sense power becomes one with what it senses. The seeing power perceives visible things through the visible forms themselves, and the intellect in act understands intelligible things through those forms when they become actual. Yet what is directly seen is not the color or shape as it exists in outside matter. We have shown that material bodies and their features are never directly present to a perceiver. What is directly present to sight is a form like the color outside. The relation of outside colors to actual sight is like the relation of outside essences to their intellectual forms. The light that the sun gives to colors is like the existence that the separate source gives to natural forms. The relation of actual visible forms to actual sight is like the relation of actual intelligibles to actual intellect. Actual intellect is its intelligibles; actual sight is its visible forms.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01145

There should be a separate substance in the world of sense that relates to actual sight and visible forms as the Active Intellect relates to intellect and intelligibles. My point here is that the Active Intellect’s action on the potential intellect resembles the sun’s action on the light that reaches sight and visible forms. That is why it is called the Active Intellect. In the account given by Aristotle’s followers, it is the tenth in rank after the First Cause among separate beings. When it gives the rational power something like the light of sight, the soul draws first and later intelligible forms from the sensible images held in imagination. Separate beings differ in how complete they are, as does the First Principle in relation to them.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01146

We have also said that the Active Intellect is of the same kind as the acquired intellect. The forms of things are always ordered in it from the noblest to the least noble. They do not exist there as separate forms or as forms lodged in it, yet they are ordered. This is another wonder. Their order in the Active Intellect differs from their order in the acquired intellect. For us, the most general ideas are first, because we learn general ideas before specific ones. But general kinds depend on the more specific kinds for their existence. We understand the specific kinds later, even though they are fuller in existence and harder for us to grasp. So the order of forms in a soul that has become intellect may at first be the reverse of their order in the Active Intellect. As the soul develops, however, it reaches the order required by its intellectual nature and by divine teaching: the noblest and brightest forms first, through their union with the knower. All natural forms are undivided in the Active Intellect but divided in matter. Aristotle is reported to have said in On the Soul: “It is no surprise that intellect, though undivided, contains undivided things, and gives matter likenesses of what is in its own being, which matter can receive only in a divided way.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01147
XXXII. Self-awareness is the self’s own act and lasts as long as the self exists
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01148

Some philosophers argue that anyone who understands himself must do so in one of two ways: either he is present to himself, or another image of him is present to him. The second option cannot be right. The image would either match him in kind or differ from him. If it matched him and existed within him, the two would have nothing to distinguish them—not in what they are, in the features that follow from their nature, or in any other respect. They could not be two, though the argument assumes that they are. That is a contradiction. If the image differed from him in kind, its presence would make him understand the thing from which the image came, not himself. So self-understanding must come from the self’s own presence to itself. It must continue for as long as the self exists. That is their argument.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01149

I find this one of the weakest arguments. Two individuals of the same kind are distinguished by their particular ways of existing. Individual human beings differ in this way. The same is true of a mental image of a human being and actual people: they differ in how they exist. According to these philosophers, the image exists in the mind as a feature of something else, while a person outside the mind exists in himself. There is nothing impossible about the same nature existing outside the mind as a substance and in the mind as a feature of something else. So an intellect could understand its own nature through a matching image without anything impossible following from it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01150

We often form an image of ourselves, and an image of ourselves thinking about ourselves. If it were impossible to understand oneself through an image distinct from oneself, we could never do this. But we do. So the argument fails.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01151

The better account begins by recognizing that a thing’s reality is its existence in some particular way. No individual existence can be understood except through that existence being present in itself, as we have explained before. If an intellect understood itself through an additional image, its existence and the image’s existence would be different. The self is a substance, while the image is a feature of something else; these are different ways of existing. The case would be like one person understanding another who shares the same human nature.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01152

There is another argument, given earlier by the author of The Pointers. Any mental image is universal, either actually or potentially, even if it is limited by many further conditions. But the self that understands is a particular person outside the mind. We also know ourselves as individuals who cannot be shared with anyone else. So this kind of self-knowledge cannot come from another image. It must come from the very existence of the self.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01153
At the end of The Pointers, he explains this point in the first person:
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01154

“I set aside everything else and looked at myself. I found that I am: I am existence. Along with this, I found that I am not in a subject, which is one way of describing a substance, and that I have relations to a body, which is one way of describing the soul. The relations to the body turned out to be outside me. Not being in a subject is a negative description. If ‘substance’ has another meaning, I do not grasp it, though I grasp myself and am not absent from myself. I have no defining feature. I know myself simply because I am not absent from myself. If I had a defining feature or some special quality beyond existence, I would perceive it when I perceive myself, since nothing is closer to me. When I examine myself closely, I find only existence and awareness. Since I differ from other things through features and awareness, nothing remains but existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01155

“If ‘awareness’ means something definite beyond what has just been said, it is awareness of something. But I am not made up of my awareness of myself, since that awareness is myself, or of my awareness of something else, since that is not essential to me. My readiness to understand is only a passing feature. Anyone who understands himself through the idea ‘I’ finds, on examining what that ‘I’ refers to, only the existence of someone who perceives himself. That existence is itself the one who perceives. It is not hidden from itself, because it is free of matter. This is what the ‘I’ truly refers to.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01156
“If someone asks, ‘Is there some distinguishing feature of you that you do not know?’ I answer: ‘If I understand what “I” means, then whatever remains unknown to me is something other than me.’”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01157

Someone objected: “Then your existence must be necessary, but it is not.” I replied: “Necessary existence is pure existence, without any limit or lack. My existence is incomplete, like the light of a ray compared with sunlight. A difference in completeness does not require another feature to distinguish the two. Possibility is a lack in my existence; necessity is the perfection of an existence beyond which there can be none.” That is the end of his words.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01158

This is a strong and carefully worked-out argument. We have already explained why caused beings are not necessary in themselves: they exist through dependence on another. Their necessity is not eternal; it lasts only while the divine reality gives existence to the intermediaries, and through them to the later beings.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01159

Let us return to our subject: a thing’s awareness of itself is its very self, and the self is always aware of itself. One sign of this is that if people observe their own states, they find that their awareness of themselves lasts as long as they do. Whenever we set out to think or to move, we do not intend merely to think or move in general. We intend a particular act of thought or movement that comes from us and takes place in us.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01160

The same is true of movement. Someone fleeing from an enemy, heat, or cold is not fleeing from an enemy or heat in general, but from a particular enemy or a particular heat that has reached him. Knowing that the heat or cold has reached him already includes awareness of himself. Likewise, anyone who chooses to do something or seek a pleasure does not intend merely that the act happen; he intends to do it himself. Nor does he seek pleasure in general, but a particular pleasure for himself. All of this rests on his awareness of himself. So it is clear that a person’s knowledge of himself is his first and earliest knowledge, and is always present, never leaving him.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01161

No one can say that I know myself by way of my actions—that I first infer myself from what I do. If I infer myself from action in general, then all I establish is that there is some agent, not that the agent is me. If I infer myself from an action of my own, I must already know myself before I can know that the action is mine. Otherwise, I would have to know myself only after knowing myself, which is circular reasoning. So a person’s self-knowledge does not come by way of his own action.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01162

Nor does using someone else’s action as evidence give us knowledge of ourselves. We know a thing either through itself, through its cause, through its effect, or through something caused by its cause, as in different kinds of proof. But something that is neither a cause nor an effect of a thing, nor an effect of its cause, cannot give us knowledge of that thing.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01163
XXXIII. Anyone who understands something must be free of matter
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01164

The proof follows from what we have already established. Understanding means that the form of the thing understood exists in the one who understands it. But an intelligible form cannot be divided into measurable parts in any way, and it cannot have a position in space, either in itself or because of something else. Blackness, for example, is not divided in itself, but it can be divided along with the body in which it exists. A point has a position only because it belongs to a line. But something that cannot be divided or located in any way cannot exist in a material thing that has a position. So an intelligible form cannot exist in a material thing. The converse follows: anything that understands an intelligible form must be free of matter. This is what we wanted to prove. The usual view is that understanding occurs when the intelligible form exists in the intellect as something received by it. Our view is that the intellect and the form become one. On our view, the proof is even clearer, since something without a position cannot become one with something that has a position.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01165

You might object: “We have established that predication means being one in existence. Yet we predicate broader kinds and species of bodily individuals. We say that Zayd, ʿAmr, and a horse are animals. The universal idea of ‘animal’ is indivisible and has no position, while each individual is divisible and located in space. It seems, then, that something indivisible must become one with something divisible, and something without a position with something that has one.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01166

That is not what happens. Meanings as they exist in the mind—as universal ideas—are not present in outside individuals in that same way. A broader kind considered as a broader kind, as a nature understood universally and shared by many, is not found in each individual in that form. The same is true of a species, a defining feature, and other ideas. What exists together with outside individuals is their natural kind considered just as it is, without being called either divisible or indivisible. In reality, it is divided, just as it exists in reality even though, considered simply in itself, it is neither called existent nor nonexistent. This does not conflict with what we have said. We mean that something actually indivisible cannot be one with something actually divided. A natural kind—the nature considered just as it is—is not like that.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01167

You might also object: “Prime matter is immaterial in itself, yet it receives size, dimensions, and position. If a subject with no position and no parts can receive something measurable and located, why can’t the reverse happen? Why can’t an intellect with a position receive an intelligible form that has no position?”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01168

The answer is the same as before. Prime matter is not really free of size or position. It is bodily, because its existence depends on bodily form, which comes before it. Measurable size is not something added only after matter is already fully real. So matter is free of size and position only in the sense that it is a potential subject, not in reality. The intelligible form, by contrast, is actually indivisible and has no position.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01169

We can also show that an intelligible form is indivisible, though this is clear to the mind from experience. Take the meaning of “rational animal,” or the statement that “one is half of two.” Neither is in a place or a body, and we cannot point to it with the senses and say it is here or there. Still, philosophers have offered a proof.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01170

If an intelligible meaning could be divided, it would have to divide either into parts that differ in nature or into parts that are alike. If the parts differed, the division would have to end in something indivisible; otherwise, the thing would be made of infinitely many basic parts, which is impossible. So, in understanding any intelligible meaning, the mind would have to grasp an indivisible part.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01171

If the parts were alike, the intelligible whole would divide into two parts similar to the whole. In that case, either each part is needed for the whole to be understood, or each part can be understood on its own, just as the whole can. The first possibility fails for three reasons. First, each part would have to be separate from the whole in the way a condition is separate from what depends on it. Putting the two parts together would produce something beyond the parts—perhaps a shape or a number—so the parts would not be parts of one and the same nature.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01172

Second, if the whole could be understood only when both parts were present, then the intelligible whole would be divisible. But we assumed that it was indivisible. Third, before division, the two parts would not yet exist separately, so the conditions for understanding the whole would not be met. It could not be understood, though we assumed that it was.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01173

The other possibility is that both parts are present, but each is also understandable on its own, like a body whose parts can each be bodies. This also fails. The intelligible form is present in the smallest amount that can be supposed to be the thing itself. Any further parts would add nothing needed to complete it. So it would be impossible to form a purely intellectual image without some unrelated feature attached to it. Yet, on the philosophers’ account, understanding means stripping away such unrelated features. Every divisible thing is made up of parts, and each part is an instance of the same kind as the whole. The kind is present in each part along with features that do not belong to the kind itself. So an intelligible idea shared by many cannot be a quantity or have a quantity.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01174

An intelligible form cannot have a position either. If it did, it would either be divisible or indivisible. If divisible, we have already shown that this is impossible. If indivisible, it would be like a point: located at the end of a measurable thing or itself the end of that thing. But an end is not a thing that exists on its own, while understanding is something real. Anything that exists at the end of another thing is, strictly speaking, a feature of that end, not of the whole thing. The same question then arises about the end itself. In reality, an endpoint is not in an extended object just because the object is extended; it belongs to it only insofar as the object stops there. A point does not belong to a line simply as a length, nor does a line belong to a surface simply as an area, nor a surface to a body simply as something with size. Each boundary belongs to the thing only insofar as it ends there. Knowledge is not like this. So if an indivisible intelligible form had a position, the thing in which it existed would not understand it in itself or because of an absence or boundary. Understanding is a perfection of something that exists, not of something that is absent.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01175

If the intellect were located in one part of the person, the person would not understand with his whole self, but only with that part. Then one and the same person would both know and not know the same thing. That is impossible.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01176
XXXIV. The one who perceives imagined forms must also be free of this material world
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01177

This claim differs from the view of most philosophers, including Avicenna and those who follow him. But what matters is proof; truth is known through proof, not through the authority of people. The senses cannot settle what belongs to the intellect; the intelligible is not ruled by what the senses perceive, but rules over it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01178

Here is the proof. Imagine a square surrounding a circle whose diameter is as large as that of the greatest sphere. The imagined square could either be related to something outside the mind as though it were a shape taken from it—but it is not such a shape—or it could be a shape held in brain matter. But the brain matter is already occupied by a much smaller shape. One piece of matter cannot at the same time hold a tiny size and a vastly greater one, or take on two different shapes at once.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01179

The brain’s shape and size are natural to it. The imagined shape, however, can be made as large or small as the soul wishes, like other images and forms. It can also grow in the imagination and expand as far as the soul chooses. A natural body cannot grow except by receiving more matter from outside. So this imagined size does not belong to brain matter or to any other outside body.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01180

The relation between the faculty that perceives the image and the image itself is therefore neither the relation between a holder and something lodged in it, nor the relation between one located thing and another. The faculty must have some relation to the image. That relation is either spatial—like being beside or facing something—or not spatial. The first option is impossible: the imagined shape is not above or below the person, to his right or left, in front or behind him. So the relation must be nonspatial. We have already seen that it is not a matter of receiving the image, with the imagined shape as a form in the faculty. Nor can the faculty be a form of the image, since something that perceives only potentially cannot be the form of something that already perceives in act. So the relation must be that of cause and effect. But the imagined shape cannot be the cause of the perceiving faculty: measurable quantities are not efficient causes of things distinct from themselves.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01181

Also, the faculty remains in us while an imagined image can disappear and return. So the imaginative faculty must produce the image, or help produce it, or take part in producing it. If it were material, it could act only through a spatial relation. Anything that acts through a spatial relation can affect only something that is located in relation to it or to its material basis. Fire heats only what is next to it; the sun lights only what faces it. Yet an imagined image has no place in any direction of this world.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01182

An imagined image also appears all at once. A bodily faculty cannot already be related to the image it will produce before that image exists; no relation to something nonexistent is possible. Philosophers have shown that a bodily cause must have a relation to its effect before the effect exists, either in time or in its own order of being. It must have a spatial relation to the matter from which the effect will arise, as fire and the sun do. But imagined forms have no matter of their own. So a bodily power cannot produce them in any way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01183
Since the imaginative faculty’s relation to these forms is neither spatial nor nonexistent, it must be their nonbodily source. It is therefore free of matter and its features.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01184

To sum up: an imagined form has no position. So it cannot exist in something that has a position, either as something received there or as something separated from it in space. The faculty that perceives it must be free of matter. This faculty is not the intellect, because the intellect understands universal ideas, which cannot be divided. Nor is the intellect, when it understands a universal, the same as the power that perceives imagined forms. So the power that perceives images in the imagination is a different power from the intellect. This shows that imagination is free of matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01185

Plato the Divine relied on another proof to show that the soul is free of matter. We imagine things that do not exist outside us, such as a sea of quicksilver or a mountain of ruby. We distinguish these imagined images from anything we have seen outside ourselves. These images must exist in some way. When we imagine Zayd and see him inwardly, we know there is a difference between that image and the one we saw with our eyes. If the imagined images did not exist in any way, we could not make this distinction.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01186

Their place cannot be a body. Our whole body is small compared with the huge images we can imagine. How could a large image fit into such a small body? Nor can we say that some images are in our bodies and others in the air around us. Air is not part of our bodies, nor is it a tool the soul uses for imagining. If it were, the soul would feel pain when the air broke apart, and we would notice changes in the air as we notice changes in our bodies.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01187

So the place of these images must be something nonbodily: the rational soul. This was Plato’s argument for the soul’s freedom from matter. It is a powerful proof for what we want to establish. But philosophers took it to prove that the soul belongs to the separate world of intellect, and that does not follow from this proof or similar ones. I have not found a clear account in the philosophers’ books of what it means for imagination to be free of this material world, while the intellect and what it understands are free of both the imaginal world and this one. This is among the things God has shown and taught me; I thank Him greatly for this gift. Two objections have been raised against this proof.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01188

The first is that imagined images must have dimensions and extension. Otherwise, they would not be imagined images. When we imagine a square, one side must be distinct from another. This means it has a particular shape and position. If that shape existed in the soul, then either the soul would take that shape and become square, or it would not. If the soul became square, it would not be free of matter. But if it did not become square, then the square image would not exist in it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01189

The author of The Investigations says that this is a very strong objection, and that he has not found an answer fit to include in his book. I answer that an image need not be present to the one who knows it by being received into it. It can be present in one of three ways: by being identical with it, as when the soul knows itself; by existing in it as a feature, as when the soul knows its own states and, according to the usual view, when intelligible forms are received by the intellect; or by being caused by it, as when God knows possible things through their detailed forms. The soul’s knowledge of imagined forms belongs to this third kind.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01190

This also resolves the usual puzzle about mental images. If the soul imagines roundness, must it become round? Philosophers say there is no difference between saying “this thing is a sphere” and “the form of a sphere is in it.” The answer is that imagined images are present to the soul as things seen in a mirror are present to us. They are not imprinted in the mirror or present in the air, and they are not identical with the material object whose image we see. We have shown that material forms are not themselves what perceives. The reflected images are suspended forms, not imprinted in the soul but present in another material thing outside it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01191

The second objection is this: if prime matter, which has no body or bodily features, can receive an image with dimensions, then a small body such as part of the brain should be even more able to receive a great image. A large and a small shape are more alike than a great shape and something with no shape at all. So large images and shapes could be received by a small bodily power, and their presence in a perceiving power would not prove that it is immaterial.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01192

My answer is as I indicated earlier. Prime matter is not actually free of matter or size in reality. In itself, it exists only as a possibility and has no definite character—not even the character of being indivisible, like a point or an intellect, or of being divisible, like magnitudes and bodies. Yet in reality it cannot be without one or the other; it receives either kind of form. But something that already has a definite character cannot receive a form that is inherently without size, such as unity or a point, or a form with a different size. So their objection fails.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01193

There is another reason why a great image cannot be contained in a small body. If two sizes are laid over each other, they must either be equal or differ in size. If they differ, the larger has a part that extends beyond the smaller. So if a great shape were imprinted in a small body, only the part equal to the body’s size could be received, and the rest would extend beyond it. That makes it impossible for a large size to exist within a body of smaller size. The imagined image also cannot be in a wholly separate, immaterial subject, as some who interpret Plato’s proof claim. We have already explained that something with no size cannot be spatially joined to something with size. This is not like the relation between a magnitude and prime matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01194

Here is another proof that imagination is free of matter. We judge that blackness and whiteness are opposites. The one who makes this judgment must have both before him. So we have shown that blackness and whiteness must exist in the mind or be present to it. It is obvious that they cannot exist together in a body or other material subject. Therefore, the place where they are present must not be a body or bodily thing. The power that perceives such particular images cannot be the intellect, since these images cannot be universal ideas. So the imaginative power is free of matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01195

Someone might object: “Blackness and whiteness are opposed by their very nature. Wherever they occur, they must be opposed. Why must they be in a physical subject?” I answer that perhaps they are opposed only in subjects that can be affected by each of them. When blackness exists in a body, it changes the body and causes certain effects, such as narrowing the pupil. When whiteness exists there, it causes different effects. But the perceiving subject is not changed by them in this way. Each can come and go, and they can occur or disappear together.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01196

That would be the case if imagination received them. But, as I have explained, the images exist for the soul through the soul’s activity, not through passive reception. The soul’s relation to them is one of producing them, not being affected by them. Even if it did receive them, its capacity to receive them would be inseparable from its capacity to produce them, as with the knowledge of separate beings. In short, opposites conflict only when they exist in a material subject that can be affected by them. So there is no contradiction in their being together in a nonmaterial subject or in a higher substance.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01197

Another objection says: “When we imagine blackness, whiteness, heat, or cold, it is only their images that exist in us, not blackness, whiteness, heat, or cold themselves. So the soul does not become hot, cold, black, or white.” I answer: Do these images really have the nature of blackness and whiteness? If they do, then the soul would indeed become hot or cold, black or white, straight or round, and so would be a body. If they do not, then perceiving things cannot mean that the nature of what is perceived is received in the one who perceives it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01198

Our direct experience tells us that when we imagine or see these things, we see the very same blackness, whiteness, or heat that we sensed outside. The truth, as we have explained, is that the soul produces these images. This relation is stronger than the relation of a passive subject to something it receives: producing something is necessary, while receiving it is only possible.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01199

Here is another proof. A body or bodily thing can have opposites at the same time in different parts. One part can be black while another is white; one part hot while another is cold. One part can face something while another does not. But the soul cannot know and not know the same particular thing at the same time. We cannot know Zayd’s writing and be ignorant of it at once. The same is true of desire and anger, love and dislike: one person cannot desire something and be angry with it, or long for it and recoil from it, in the same respect. This shows that the powers of understanding and desire are not bodily. They are not the intellect, either, because they perceive particular images rather than universal ideas. So they are free of this material world, though they do not reach the world of intelligible forms.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01200

Someone may ask whether the soul itself could be an indivisible point and so bodily. But a point is an endpoint, and an endpoint cannot receive something as a subject. The true subject would have to be the extended thing whose boundary it is; that would be measurable, which we have already ruled out.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01201

Someone may object that, according to the philosophers, opposites cannot be present in different parts of the heavens. So perhaps the heart or the subtle spirit within it is like the heavens: a body that cannot receive opposites. I answer that the heavens do not receive some opposites because they cannot be affected by one of them. Air, for example, cannot be black or white, because it cannot receive either quality. But if a thing can receive one of two opposites, it can receive the other in another part. Also, the heavens do have other opposites in different parts: one part touches a sphere while another does not; one part is north while another is south, or east while another is west. So the heavens are still bodily.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01202

These are strong and decisive proofs. They will be very useful for understanding the next life. I will return to them in the discussions of the soul and the afterlife. This principle is especially important because it resolves many difficulties. For example, Alexander believed that souls which never reached intellect in act perish. Avicenna struggled to answer this in one of his works, The Ten Proofs. If human beings had no other nonbodily power besides intellect, then a potential intellect would perish when the body perishes.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01203
Nothing of the human being would remain, though the revealed laws teach that every human soul survives—happy or unhappy, complete or incomplete, learned or ignorant.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01204
XXXV. The human soul’s understanding is not essential or necessary to it
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01205

This passage comes from some who believed that rational souls existed before their bodies. Although the view is attributed to established philosophers such as Plato and his followers, it may be understood as a subtle symbol beyond the reach of most people. The human soul has different stages, some before its connection with the body and others after it comes into being.
